lesson.title: Planning Ahead: How Many People Do You Need to Survey?
lesson.summary: Solving the margin-of-error formula for n lets researchers calculate, before collecting any data, the minimum sample size needed to guarantee a target margin of error at a chosen confidence level.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter showed that sample size is one of the levers controlling a confidence interval's width. That relationship can be run in reverse: instead of computing the margin of error that a given sample size produces, you can specify the margin of error you want and solve for the sample size required to achieve it. Starting from margin of error equals z star times sqrt(p-hat(1-p-hat)/n), algebra gives n = (z star divided by ME) squared, times p-hat times (1 minus p-hat). Since a sample size must be a whole number, and rounding down could produce a margin of error slightly larger than intended, the convention is to always round the result up to the next whole person.

One wrinkle is that this formula needs a value of p-hat before you have collected any data. If a prior estimate exists, from an earlier study or a similar population, use it. If no prior estimate is available, use p-hat = 0.5, because p-hat(1-p-hat) is maximized at 0.5 (its largest possible value is 0.25), which produces the largest, most conservative required sample size, guaranteeing your margin of error target is met no matter what the true proportion turns out to be.

Worked example: a campaign wants to estimate the percentage of the electorate that supports its candidate to within 3 percentage points, that is, a margin of error of 0.03, at 95 percent confidence, and has no prior polling data to draw on. Using the conservative p-hat = 0.5, n = (1.96 divided by 0.03) squared times (0.5 times 0.5). First, 1.96/0.03 is about 65.333, and squaring that gives about 4268.44. Multiplying by 0.25 gives about 1067.11. Rounding up, the campaign needs to survey at least 1068 people to guarantee a margin of error no larger than 3 percentage points at 95 percent confidence.

If instead the campaign had a prior estimate to lean on, say an earlier poll found p-hat = 0.55 (matching the voter survey used in earlier chapters), the calculation would use 0.55 times 0.45 = 0.2475 in place of 0.25: n = 4268.44 times 0.2475, which is about 1056.4, rounding up to 1057. Notice this is a smaller required sample than the conservative 1068, because 0.2475 is slightly less than the worst-case value of 0.25, so less data is needed to pin down a proportion that is not right at 0.5. This illustrates the same principle from the previous chapter in reverse: whenever variability is lower, you need less data to hit the same precision target.
